questions.q: Who were the nomadic and mobile communities of medieval India? Describe their role.
answer: Alongside settled villagers, many people led mobile lives as nomads and travelling groups.

answer.text: They moved from place to place with their herds, living on milk and animal produce, and exchanged wool, ghee and cattle for grain, cloth and utensils sold in settled areas.
The most important trader-nomads were the Banjaras, who moved in caravans called tandas. They carried grain over long distances, supplying towns and provisioning armies on the march.
Entertainers, peddlers and travelling craftspeople also moved from town to town.

answer: These mobile communities linked distant regions and were vital to trade and the food supply.

questions.q: Describe the Gond and Ahom kingdoms.

answer.text: The Gonds lived in Gondwana in central India and practised shifting cultivation. Some Gond chiefs built kingdoms, notably Garha Katanga. When the Mughals attacked, Rani Durgawati resisted bravely before being defeated. As they grew powerful, Gond rulers were given kshatriya status and genealogies by Brahmanas.

The Ahoms migrated into Assam from present-day Myanmar in the thirteenth century and built a strong state, suppressing the older bhuiyan chiefs. They used firearms, organised labour through the paik system of forced service, and kept detailed chronicles called buranjis.

answer: Both show how tribal societies could create durable kingdoms and merge with wider caste society.
